cells.tense: You are seeing this whole, and what you see is still open to what comes next.
cells.ask: Tell one person the part of the pattern that touches them — the plain version, not the finished one — and stay in the conversation after you've said it.
cells.core:
You can see the shape of a thing and still stand inside it with the person it involves. That's the whole trick, and you're doing it. You don't name what's true about someone from a distance and call it done — you stay close enough that what you see keeps changing as they move. The not-knowing is still there at the end of the sentence, and you leave it there on purpose.

That's a harder seat than it sounds, because seeing clearly and holding somebody are usually sold as a trade. When it's going well the person can feel both at once: that you've seen them, and that you haven't finished with them. Keeping it costs something — you don't get the clean version where you're simply right. Say the piece that belongs to the person in front of you, then let the next sentence come from them.
cells.sheetLine: You can see the whole thing and stay next to them.
cells.verb: seeing the whole of a thing while still standing inside it
cells.place: beside someone, in the same room, close enough to be moved and not dissolved

cells.tense: You are reading people ahead of the moment they are actually in, and the verdict arrives before they do.
cells.ask: Next time you catch the ending early, keep it to yourself for a day and do one thing with the person that has nothing to do with what you've decided about them.
cells.core:
You've started arriving at the conclusion before the person has finished being in the room. It comes out as a certainty about where someone's heading, delivered like help. From inside it feels like seeing truly. From the other chair it lands as a sentence already passed, and there's nothing left for them to say.

You take in all the layers and skip the part where you're still in it with them. The verdict is the whole point normally — right now it's a closed door. When you know what's true and it leaves the person room to be more than what you saw, that's the good version. Coming back doesn't mean seeing less. It means saying it unfinished, so the other person can answer.

cells.tense: What you noticed back then never got said in the room, and that unsaid thing is where you left it.
cells.ask: Pick one person and say one true thing you notice about them, out loud, before the moment is over — no preface, just the sentence.
cells.core:
You can see a pattern forming and you've stopped handing it over. Something about how you read a room got quiet, and quiet reads as ease from the outside. Meanwhile you keep noticing and none of it gets said. Nobody gets told what you saw.

Waiting for the read to get more solid doesn't help — it only gets heavier. The next open moment is the material. Stay with one person past your first read of them, and let the second one show up while they're still there. The pull to keep waiting for a better time is not caution. It's a door you're parked at. Open the next ordinary one.

cells.tense: Reading the room as you go is already shaping how this conversation turns, and it's going down in your account as just being reasonable.
cells.ask: Say out loud that you noticed something — one line, in the moment — and let that count as contribution instead of moderation.
cells.core:
You're already shaping how this goes — you feel where the room is heading and you adjust before anyone says a word, and the adjusting is doing most of the work in the conversation. Then you tell yourself you're just not making it weird.

Reading the room is the writing, though. Calling it being easygoing takes the credit off the one act that holds this together. When you own it, the reading is warm — it gives the person next to you somewhere to stand. Right now it's running half-lit and coming out as the careful version instead of the true one. Put one observation into the room and let it count as yours.

attempts.check: The record does not say the person has been holding recognition back from anyone in particular; the reader could reasonably say no, I never had a room where saying it went badly — so the Too Little cell locates the stillness, not a cause behind it. The asks survive that: telling one person what you see, and staying past the first read, ask nothing about history and would help even if the read is wrong. The sentence that serves the writer rather than the person is the early draft's 'you've been the one who sees it all along' — it flatters the reader's eye and tells the person nothing they can use, so it is gone. The pull to write 'recognition without finality' on glass is the other one; kept in the record's language only.
